summary: A Fox News Lifestyle guide to seeing the Northern Lights (Aurora Borealis), which are expected to be stronger than in at least a decade as the sun nears the peak of its 11-year cycle in 2024 or 2025. It lists top viewing spots in the US (Fairbanks, Lake Superior in Michigan, Priest Lake in Idaho) and Europe (Tromsø, Swedish Lapland, Jökulsárlón in Iceland). It closes with tips on geomagnetic activity, location, darkness and timing.
one_line: Guide to the best US and European places to watch the Northern Lights, plus tips on activity, location, darkness and timing.
key_facts: The Northern Lights are expected to be stronger than they have been for at least a decade over the next few months in the Northern Hemisphere, per New Scientist.
The sun is approaching the expected peak of its 11-year solar cycle in 2024 or 2025, and sunspot observations show a dramatic increase from a year earlier.
Fairbanks, Alaska, is within the auroral oval and has dark skies, making it one of the best places in the world to see the lights.
Michigan's Upper Peninsula along the south shore of Lake Superior offers some of the best viewing in the lower 48, with a 180-degree unobstructed view of the night sky looking north.
Priest Lake in far-northern Idaho has become a major spot for aurora hunters, and its marina turns out the lights so viewers can see the sky better.
Tromsø, Norway, is the third largest city north of the Arctic Circle and lies just within the Northern Lights Oval; the display can be seen from September to April.
Abisko in Swedish Lapland lies within the aurora oval, has surrounding mountains that keep skies clear, and is home to the Aurora Sky Station with an observation tower and experts.
Jökulsárlón Glacier Lagoon in Iceland has minimal light pollution, and the best viewing is during late evening and early night hours.
The Space Weather Prediction Center says the best time to see the lights is when the planetary K index is at an eight or nine and the aurora moves toward the equator.
When the geomagnetic field is active, the aurora is brighter, stronger and further from the magnetic poles.
Viewers should choose a spot with minimal tree lines or hills so the northern horizon is fully visible, and go at night away from city lights.
A full moon diminishes the apparent brightness of the aurora, but not its actual brightness.
The lights are usually on full display from September to March or April, with the best aurora typically within an hour or two of midnight (between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m. local time).
